lessons.title: Why Starship uses hot staging
lessons.card: Light the engines. Then let go.
lessons.summary: Follow the ignition, venting and separation sequence through an illustrated cutaway of the hot-staging ring.
lessons.answer: Starship ignites its engines before separating from Super Heavy. The vented ring gives the upper stage’s exhaust a route out while the two vehicles are still together.
lessons.intro: The important detail is the order of events. Follow the five stages below, then switch to cold staging to see where a coast fits into the alternative sequence.
lessons.imageAlt: SpaceX footage of Starship hot staging
lessons.diagramNote: Original schematic · not to scale · stages are illustrative, not a flight clock

stages.title: The booster carries the stack
stages.text: Super Heavy accelerates the combined vehicle. Starship is still attached above the interstage. The enlarged view follows the joint between them.
stages.cold: The stages remain attached during ascent. Both approaches begin with the booster doing the work.

stages.title: Prepare for upper-stage ignition
stages.text: The booster throttles down for staging. The ring between the stages is vented so that exhaust can escape when Starship’s engines ignite.
stages.cold: In this simplified cold-staging comparison, the booster shuts down before separation and upper-stage ignition.

stages.title: Starship ignites
stages.text: The upper-stage engines light while the vehicles are still connected. Exhaust exits through the hot-staging ring. This is the moment the cutaway highlights.
stages.cold: The upper stage separates before lighting its engines. The gap in powered flight is shown as a coast; its duration depends on the rocket.

stages.title: Separate under thrust
stages.text: Starship departs with its engines already running. The booster and ship now have separate jobs: continue the mission above, and prepare the booster’s return below.
stages.cold: After separation and any required settling sequence, the upper-stage engines ignite. The comparison shows a different event order, not a measured performance penalty.

stages.title: Continue on separate paths
stages.text: Starship continues accelerating. Super Heavy turns toward its return sequence. The hot-staging operation has ended; boostback is the next phase.
stages.cold: The upper stage continues its burn. Both methods can work; their hardware, ignition and propellant-management requirements differ.

sections.title: Why the sequence matters
sections.text: A coast creates a pause between powered phases. Igniting before separation reduces that interruption, but introduces a demanding exhaust and separation problem. The ring is part of the hardware that makes that trade possible.

sections.title: What the flight timeline tells us
sections.text: SpaceX’s Flight 14 timeline lists booster MECO at T+2:20 and hot staging at T+2:22. Those are approximate event times for that flight, not universal timings for every Starship vehicle.

misconceptions.title: The exhaust belongs to the upper stage
misconceptions.text: At the hot-staging joint, the key plume comes from Starship’s engines above the booster. The ring vents that exhaust outward.

misconceptions.title: The animation is not a flight simulation
misconceptions.text: The five stages explain the mechanism. Distances, plume shapes and playback speed are schematic; they do not predict a flight’s trajectory or payload gain.

glossary.text: The structure connecting two rocket stages.
Engine-cutoff shorthand. SpaceX’s timeline expands it here as most engines cut off.
The gas space in a propellant tank; a coast can also create a need to settle liquid before an engine start.

lessons.title: How a booster catch works
lessons.card: A landing pad that reaches out.
lessons.summary: See the return, alignment and transfer of load to the tower, with elevation and overhead views.
lessons.answer: The returning booster slows and aligns with the tower so its catch fittings can meet the arms. Once supported, the booster’s weight is carried by the tower rather than landing legs.
lessons.intro: A catch is a sequence of positioning, braking and alignment. The two views below focus on those relationships, with an enlarged view of the catch area.
lessons.imageAlt: SpaceX footage of the first Super Heavy catch
lessons.diagramNote: Original schematic · not to scale · no measured trajectory or control model
legend: Catch area: load transfers to the arms

stages.title: Return toward the launch site
stages.text: After separation, the booster’s return sequence brings it back toward the launch area. This diagram begins with the approach; it does not plot the full boostback trajectory.

stages.title: Control the approach
stages.text: The booster must reach the catch area with the required position and orientation. Compare the elevation with the overhead view: arriving at the right height alone is not enough.

stages.title: Slow for the catch
stages.text: The landing burn reduces the booster’s speed as it approaches the arms. The illustrated flame marks that phase, without assigning an engine count or a fixed burn duration.

stages.title: Meet the catch fittings
stages.text: The booster’s catch fittings and the arms must line up. The red markers identify the relationship being explained, not the tolerances of an actual flight.

stages.title: The tower carries the load
stages.text: Once supported by the arms, the booster hangs at the tower. The final view highlights the support path and turns off the landing-burn illustration.

sections.title: Why put the landing hardware on the ground?
sections.text: A tower catch moves some recovery infrastructure off the flying vehicle. It also makes the return depend on a particular facility and a tightly coordinated approach. That is the central engineering trade.

sections.title: A demonstrated milestone
sections.text: SpaceX’s fifth Starship flight demonstrated the first Super Heavy tower catch. The official film below is the reference for the broad sequence; the illustration is an explanation of that sequence, not a reconstruction of its telemetry.

misconceptions.title: The arms are not a net
misconceptions.text: The mechanism depends on alignment with the booster’s catch area. A diagram of two arms around a cylinder is not a description of the complete guidance and control system.

misconceptions.title: A booster catch does not prove a ship catch
misconceptions.text: Starship and Super Heavy are different vehicles. A completed booster catch should not be presented as confirmation of a future ship catch or an unannounced flight plan.

glossary.text: The burn that redirects the booster toward its return area.
A side view that shows height and vertical relationships.
An overhead view that shows lateral alignment.

lessons.title: Why FSD differs between cars
lessons.summary: Untangle the three things that determine a car’s feature set, then compare the tracker’s reported software branches.
lessons.answer: An FSD label does not describe every Tesla’s capabilities. Hardware, installed software, vehicle configuration and regional availability all matter. Full Self-Driving (Supervised) still requires an attentive driver.
lessons.intro: Start with the three layers in the illustration. The comparison further down uses the same maintained version data as the global FSD tracker, with its snapshot date shown explicitly.
lessons.imageAlt: Tesla footage of Full Self-Driving Supervised
lessons.diagramNote: Conceptual illustration · camera views are schematic · not Tesla’s software architecture

stages.title: Start with the vehicle
stages.text: A model name alone does not identify its complete configuration. Build date, equipment and the information shown in the vehicle are better starting points than another owner’s video.

stages.title: Identify the hardware
stages.text: Hardware generations describe the vehicle’s computing and camera configuration. A newer software announcement should not be read as a promise that every hardware generation receives the same features.

stages.title: Check the installed software
stages.text: The vehicle software build and the FSD version are different labels. Record both when comparing release notes. A reported build in a sample is not confirmation that your car has received it.

stages.title: Check the region and entitlement
stages.text: Tesla says availability can depend on configuration, hardware, software, region, model and model year. A release in one market does not establish availability in another.

stages.title: Keep the driver in the loop
stages.text: Tesla describes these features as supervised driver assistance. They do not replace the driver or make the consumer vehicle autonomous. Review the instructions for your particular car.

sections.title: Read a version comparison correctly
sections.text: The table separates hardware, FSD version and vehicle build. Different values are highlighted so you can see what actually changed. It reports the site tracker’s snapshot; it does not certify eligibility for a particular VIN.

sections.title: Use your car as the final check
sections.text: The useful question is what is installed, enabled and supported on your vehicle. Use its software screen, release notes and owner’s manual alongside the tracker. The diagram deliberately makes no claim about Tesla’s internal neural-network design.

misconceptions.title: A shared name does not mean a shared release
misconceptions.text: Two cars can show the FSD brand while running different software branches or having different supported features.

misconceptions.title: Supervised is a meaningful requirement
misconceptions.text: The driver must remain attentive. A polished route demonstration does not establish that a consumer car can operate without supervision.

glossary.text: Common hardware-generation labels used by the site’s tracker.
The installed vehicle-software identifier, distinct from an FSD version label.
The process of making a software release available to eligible vehicles over time.

lessons.title: Understanding Collision Evasion
lessons.card: A warning is not the same as an intervention.
lessons.summary: An overhead visual guide to a developing hazard, driver warnings and possible braking assistance, with the limits kept clear.
lessons.answer: Collision-assistance functions can warn or intervene in particular situations. Warning, emergency braking and engaging FSD are different behaviours; the name of one should not be used as evidence for another.
lessons.intro: This lesson explains the documented safety functions behind a hazard-response sequence. It does not certify a release-specific FSD re-engagement feature for any hardware or region.
lessons.imageAlt: Tesla driver-assistance footage; not a collision test
lessons.diagramTitle: Read the response, understand the limit
lessons.diagramNote: Illustrative scenario · not a crash test, stopping-distance model or guaranteed sequence

stages.title: A hazard develops
stages.text: The overhead view shows a vehicle ahead in the path of travel. Positions are illustrative. No distance, speed or time-to-collision should be inferred from this drawing.

stages.title: Detection has limits
stages.text: Cameras and environmental conditions affect what a system can detect. The shaded area is a visual aid, not a specification of sensor coverage or guaranteed detection.

stages.title: A warning may be issued
stages.text: Tesla describes Forward Collision Warning as a visual and audible alert. That warning is distinct from a braking command. The driver remains responsible for responding.

stages.title: Braking assistance may intervene
stages.text: Automatic Emergency Braking is a separate function that may reduce speed in certain collision situations. Its behaviour has conditions and limitations; the illustration does not show a guaranteed stop.

stages.title: The driver remains responsible
stages.text: Do not rely on an assistance system to detect every hazard or prevent a crash. Use the instructions and limitations in your vehicle’s manual, including the requirements for any supervised driving feature.

sections.title: Keep the feature names separate
sections.text: An emergency-braking feature is not proof that FSD will engage or re-engage. For a release carrying a Collision Evasion label, check its exact notes, supported hardware and region in the current software tracker.

sections.title: Why this diagram has no success score
sections.text: A successful-looking animation cannot establish real-world avoidance performance. This sequence teaches the distinction between a hazard, a warning and a possible intervention. It is not an instruction to test the system.

misconceptions.title: A warning does not promise braking
misconceptions.text: Treat the alert and an automatic intervention as separate functions with their own conditions.

misconceptions.title: A demonstration does not establish availability
misconceptions.text: A clip from another car or market does not confirm a particular feature for your vehicle.

glossary.text: An alert about a possible collision risk; distinct from automatic braking.
A function that may apply braking in defined conditions to reduce impact severity.
Assistance intended to help avoid or mitigate incidents while the driver remains responsible.
